title: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Pulmonology

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed acute pulmonary embolism: clinical probability, diagnostic pathway, interim and definitive anticoagulation, haemodynamically unstable PE, treatment setting and duration. Verified against NICE NG158, the Saudi MoH VTE guideline and FDA drug labels; ESC and AHA/ACC severity stratification not covered.
findings: NICE NG158 recommendation text and tables were read in full on 13 Oct 2026; doses and contraindications were read from US FDA labels via openFDA on the same date; the Saudi VTE guideline was read from the PMC full text.
The Saudi VTE guideline addresses only the treatment setting (outpatient versus inpatient); it does not address diagnosis, drug choice or thrombolysis.
Normal values are typical adult ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: SFDA registration and formulary not checked (SFDA register could not be reached from the authoring environment)
ESC 2019 and AHA/ACC PE guidelines could not be opened, so severity classification (including definitions of haemodynamic instability, intermediate-risk PE and sPESI thresholds) is not given
PERC criteria items and the age-adjusted D-dimer formula are not listed in NICE NG158 and are not reproduced
Doses of vitamin K antagonists, edoxaban and dabigatran not reproduced
Presenting signs of PE beyond those used in the Wells score are not listed in the cited sources
FDA labels are US labels; Saudi product information may differ

pathophysiology.summary: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the two forms of venous thromboembolism (VTE), the other being deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The practical task is to estimate clinical probability, confirm or exclude PE quickly without delaying anticoagulation, and separate haemodynamically unstable PE, which needs heparin infusion and consideration of thrombolysis, from stable PE.
keyMechanisms: VTE comprises DVT and PE and affects approximately 100 per 100,000 people per year, an estimated 25,000 people annually in Saudi Arabia (Saudi VTE guideline, Introduction).

Major risk factors for VTE are age, surgery, hospitalisation, immobility, trauma, cancer, pregnancy and puerperium, hormone use, obesity, and inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states (Saudi VTE guideline, Introduction).

Provoked PE follows a recent (within 3 months) transient major risk factor such as surgery, trauma, significant immobility, pregnancy or puerperium, or hormonal therapy; unprovoked PE has no such factor (NICE NG158, Terms used).

Concurrent DVT matters: PE and proximal DVT are treated with the same anticoagulation, and a leg vein ultrasound is considered if DVT is suspected and CT or V/Q scanning does not show PE (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.20 and 1.3.5).
Haemodynamic instability changes treatment: continuous unfractionated heparin infusion and consideration of systemic thrombolysis (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.12 and 1.6.2).

symptoms: Chest pain, shortness of breath or coughing up blood (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.15).
Signs or symptoms of DVT may coexist: a swollen or painful leg (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.22).
Neither source lists further presenting symptoms of PE.
physicalSigns: Heart rate over 100 per minute scores 1.5 on the PE Wells score (NICE NG158 Table 2).
Clinical signs of DVT (minimum leg swelling and pain on palpation of the deep veins) score 3 (NICE NG158 Table 2).

Haemodynamic status determines treatment: instability needs UFH infusion and consideration of thrombolysis (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.12 and 1.6.2). The source does not define the blood pressure or shock threshold.
redFlags: PE with haemodynamic instability: continuous UFH infusion and consider systemic thrombolytic therapy (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.12 and 1.6.2).
PE Wells score above 4 (PE likely): CTPA immediately if possible, otherwise interim therapeutic anticoagulation (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.18).
Chest pain with haemodynamic instability needs emergency referral and a search for coronary and non-coronary causes including PE (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.1.3 and 1.2.2.8).
PE that occurs during anticoagulation treatment: check adherence and other hypercoagulability before changing treatment or considering an IVC filter (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.21 and 1.7.3).
precipitants: Immobilisation for more than 3 days or surgery in the previous 4 weeks (NICE NG158 Table 2).
Previous DVT or PE (NICE NG158 Table 2).
Malignancy on treatment, treated in the last 6 months, or palliative (NICE NG158 Table 2).
Age, hospitalisation, trauma, pregnancy and puerperium, hormone use, obesity, and inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states (Saudi VTE guideline, Introduction).
Combined oral contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy counts as a provoking factor (NICE NG158, Terms used).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Chest pain with ischaemic ECG change and a rise and fall of troponin; troponin can also rise in PE, so reassess for PE when troponin is raised (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
Chest X-ray, offered to everyone with suspected PE, helps exclude other causes (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.15; NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.8).
Another life-threatening cause of chest pain to exclude; early CT is used for this (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.2.8 and 1.2.6.7). Neither source lists distinguishing symptoms.

Leg swelling and pain; the 2-level DVT Wells score of 2 points or more means DVT likely, 1 point or less unlikely (NICE NG158 Table 1). If PE is excluded but DVT is suspected, consider proximal leg vein ultrasound (Rec. 1.1.20).

differentials.condition: Another diagnosis at least as likely as PE
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: On the PE Wells score, 'alternative diagnosis less likely than PE' scores 3; if an alternative is at least as likely, those points are not scored (NICE NG158 Table 2). Think about alternatives after a negative D-dimer or imaging (Recs 1.1.20–1.1.21).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT, immediately if possible when PE is likely
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries confirms PE.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Offer immediately if possible when the PE Wells score is above 4, or after a positive D-dimer when PE is unlikely. If CTPA cannot be done immediately, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.18 and 1.1.21).
ruleIn.normalValue: No filling defect in the pulmonary arteries

ruleOut.testName: D-dimer (only if PE unlikely, Wells 4 or less)
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Venous blood or fully quantitative point-of-care test
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Positive result: proceed to CTPA or V/Q. Negative result: stop interim anticoagulation and think of alternative diagnoses.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Result available within 4 hours if possible. Consider a point-of-care test if laboratory facilities are not immediately available, and choose a fully quantitative test. Consider an age-adjusted threshold over 50 years (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.12–1.1.14 and 1.1.21).
ruleOut.normalValue: Below the assay threshold (age-adjusted threshold may be used over 50 years; the source gives no numeric cut-off)

clinicalManagement.title: Initial assessment and clinical probability
actions: Take the medical history, examine, and offer a chest X-ray to exclude other causes in anyone with chest pain, shortness of breath or coughing up blood (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.15).
If suspicion of PE is low and other diagnoses are feasible, consider the PERC rule to decide whether any further investigation is needed (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.16).
If PE is suspected, score the 2-level PE Wells score (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.17).
If signs or symptoms of both DVT and PE are present, base the choice of investigation on clinical judgement (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.22).
If haemodynamically unstable, go to the unstable branch below without waiting for imaging.

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnostic pathway by Wells score
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day; D-dimer result within 4 hours if possible
actions: Choose the pathway from the PE Wells score. Interim therapeutic anticoagulation covers any delay (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.18 and 1.1.21).
Offer CTPA immediately if possible (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.18).
If CTPA is unsuitable (contrast allergy, estimated creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, or high irradiation risk), assess V/Q SPECT, or planar V/Q if SPECT is unavailable (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.18).
If no imaging can be done immediately, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.18).
Offer D-dimer with the result within 4 hours if possible; if not available in 4 hours, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation while waiting (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.21).
D-dimer positive: follow the PE likely pathway (CTPA or V/Q) (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.21).
D-dimer negative: stop interim anticoagulation, think of alternative diagnoses, and tell the person PE is not likely, discussing symptoms and when to seek help (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.21).
Consider proximal leg vein ultrasound if DVT is suspected. If DVT is not suspected, stop interim anticoagulation and think about alternative diagnoses (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.20).

clinicalManagement.title: Interim therapeutic anticoagulation
actions: Choose an interim anticoagulant that can be continued if PE is confirmed (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.3).
Take baseline FBC, renal and hepatic function, PT and APTT; do not wait for results before starting; review and act on them within 24 hours (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.4).
Direct oral anticoagulants and some LMWHs were off label for suspected DVT or PE in March 2020 (NICE NG158, note to Rec. 1.3.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirmed PE: haemodynamically stable
actions: Offer anticoagulation for at least 3 months (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.5).

Offer apixaban or rivaroxaban. If neither is suitable: LMWH for at least 5 days followed by dabigatran or edoxaban, or LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on 2 consecutive readings, then the VKA alone (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.8).
Do not routinely give UFH with a VKA unless there is renal impairment, established renal failure or increased bleeding risk (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.9).
Do not offer systemic thrombolysis to haemodynamically stable people, with or without right ventricular dysfunction (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.6.3).

Consider outpatient treatment of low-risk PE using a validated risk stratification tool (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.2.1). The Saudi panel suggests early over late discharge for low-risk acute PE and advocates a validated tool such as the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (Saudi VTE guideline, Question 2 and Discussion).

branches.condition: Renal impairment (estimated creatinine clearance 15 to 50 mL/min)
actions: Offer apixaban, rivaroxaban, LMWH for at least 5 days then edoxaban (or dabigatran if clearance is 30 mL/min or above), or LMWH or UFH with a VKA (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.13).

branches.condition: Established renal failure (estimated creatinine clearance below 15 mL/min)
actions: Offer LMWH, UFH, or LMWH or UFH concurrently with a VKA followed by the VKA alone (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.14).
Anticoagulate for 3 to 6 months and review; consider a DOAC, otherwise LMWH alone or LMWH with a VKA (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.15–1.3.18).
LMWH concurrently with a VKA for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on 2 consecutive readings, then the VKA alone (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.20).

branches.condition: Weight below 50 kg or above 120 kg
actions: Consider regular monitoring of therapeutic levels and follow the product information and local protocol (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.3.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirmed PE with haemodynamic instability
actions: Offer continuous UFH infusion and consider systemic pharmacological thrombolytic therapy (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.12 and 1.6.2).

If anticoagulation is contraindicated, consider a mechanical intervention (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.19). Consider an IVC filter when anticoagulation is contraindicated, and remove it once anticoagulation is established (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.7.2).

If PE occurs despite anticoagulation, check adherence, address other sources of hypercoagulability, then increase the dose or change to an anticoagulant with a different mode of action before considering an IVC filter (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.21 and 1.7.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Duration and review
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At 3 months (3 to 6 months with active cancer)
actions: Discuss benefits and risks of continuing, stopping or changing the anticoagulant (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.1).
Provoked PE: consider stopping at 3 months if the provoking factor has gone and the course was uncomplicated, giving written advice and contact details (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.2).

Unprovoked PE: consider continuing beyond 3 months, balancing recurrence against bleeding risk; HAS-BLED may be used, and stopping should be discussed if the score is 4 or more and cannot be modified (NICE NG158 Recs 1.4.3 and 1.4.6).
If the person declines anticoagulation, consider aspirin 75 mg or 150 mg daily (off label in March 2020) (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.11).
Review general health, recurrence risk, bleeding risk and preferences at least once a year (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.12).

For unprovoked PE, review history, bloods and examination for cancer; do not do further cancer investigations without relevant symptoms or signs (NICE NG158 Recs 1.8.1–1.8.2). Do not test for thrombophilia after provoked PE (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.9.2).

medicationPlan.note: Doses for apixaban, rivaroxaban, heparin, alteplase and enoxaparin come from US FDA labels; NICE NG158 gives choices of agent and duration but not doses. Vitamin K antagonist, edoxaban and dabigatran doses are not reproduced. Check SFDA registration, local protocol and the hospital formulary.

learningObjectives: Estimate clinical probability with the PE Wells score and choose D-dimer or imaging accordingly.
Start interim anticoagulation when imaging or D-dimer is delayed.
Treat haemodynamically unstable PE with UFH infusion and consider thrombolysis, and stable PE with a DOAC.
keyPoints: PE Wells: above 4 = likely (CTPA immediately); 4 or less = unlikely (D-dimer within 4 hours).
Do not wait for baseline blood results before starting anticoagulation.
Apixaban or rivaroxaban first line for stable PE; at least 3 months of treatment.
No systemic thrombolysis in haemodynamically stable PE.
pitfalls: Delaying anticoagulation while waiting for imaging when a scan or D-dimer cannot be done in time (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.18 and 1.1.21).
Using D-dimer when the PE Wells score is above 4 (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.18 and 1.1.21).
Using thrombolysis in a stable patient with right ventricular dysfunction (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.6.3).
Testing for thrombophilia after provoked PE or investigating for cancer without symptoms or signs (NICE NG158 Recs 1.8.2 and 1.9.2).
Forgetting that heparins are of animal origin and DOACs contain lactose from cow's milk when counselling people with religious or ethical concerns (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.5.3).

patientEducation: Give verbal and written information on how to use anticoagulants, how long to take them, side effects, interactions with other medicines, foods and alcohol, monitoring, dental treatment, pregnancy, sports and travel, and when to seek help (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.5.1).
Give an anticoagulant alert card specific to the treatment and advise carrying it at all times (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.5.2).
Heparins are of animal origin, and apixaban and rivaroxaban contain lactose from cow's milk; discuss with people who have religious, ethical or dietary concerns (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.5.3).
If anticoagulation is stopped, explain the risk of recurrence and give written symptom information and contact details of a thrombosis team (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.2).
lifestyleAndDiet: Explain how foods and alcohol can affect oral anticoagulation (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.5.1).
The sources give no further lifestyle or diet recommendations for PE.
mdtReferrals: Thrombosis service or expert team with direct contact and out-of-hours information for people treated as outpatients (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.2.4).
Specialist or multidisciplinary advice for extremes of body weight, renal impairment, active cancer or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.7 and 1.3.11).
Interventional radiology or vascular teams where an IVC filter is considered, with a removal strategy documented first (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.7.4).
dischargeCriteria: Low-risk PE on a validated risk stratification tool, with an agreed monitoring and follow-up plan (NICE NG158 Recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.4).
Anticoagulation started, baseline blood tests reviewed within 24 hours, and information and an alert card given (NICE NG158 Recs 1.3.4 and 1.5.1–1.5.2).
The Saudi panel notes that early discharge needs 24-hour clinic coverage (Saudi VTE guideline, Question 2).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 3 months (3 to 6 months with active cancer) to decide whether to stop, continue or change the anticoagulant (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.1), then at least annually while on long-term anticoagulation or aspirin (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.4.12).

guidelineComparison.note: The two documents agree on the direction for low-risk PE; the Saudi guideline is narrower in scope and does not address drug choice. The Saudi evidence rested on 2 trials (471 participants) for PE, with moderate-quality evidence of possible small increases in recurrence and major bleeding that were imprecise (Question 2).
